    It was wonderful to learn from the next generation of leaders at the University of Global Health Equity. Building on my friend Paul Farmer’s vision of health equity, institutions like UGHE are helping train the next generation of doctors and public health leaders to strengthen the health systems their communities rely on, while networks like COMS-A are helping elevate these ideas across the continent. 
    University of Global Health Equity

    University of Global Health Equity

    4d
    Bill Gates shared this
    At the inaugural Paul E. Farmer #ButaroDialogues on Health Equity and Innovation, Mr. Bill Gates reflected on the legacy of Paul Farmer, whose vision and commitment continue to shape the work and spirit of Butaro. Recalling his journey with Dr. Paul, including visits to health facilities such as Rwinkwavu Hospital, Mr. Gates paid tribute to Dr. Paul’s enduring belief that “where you live should never determine whether you live.” He described UGHE as a testament to what Paul believed was possible and shared that, while he deeply misses Paul, it is comforting to see his legacy continue here in Butaro. In his lecture, Mr. Gates also recognized Rwanda’s remarkable progress in strengthening health systems, including significant reductions in child mortality and maternal deaths. He commended the country’s leadership in healthcare innovation and highlighted the importance of working together to ensure that proven solutions reach the people who need them most. “It is not a mystery what we need to do. We understand the challenge, and we have the tools to act.” Acknowledging that the world is facing a difficult period for global health, he noted that leaders must find ways to achieve more with fewer resources. He also warned that emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence, must not become concentrated in wealthier countries or benefit only those who already have access. “AI should not only be available to those who already have access; we should bring AI to those who need it most.” Mr. Gates commended #UGHE’s One Health approach to making health more equitable and highlighted The Consortium of Medical Schools-Africa (COMS-A) as an important platform bringing medical schools together for better outcomes. He emphasized that institutions like UGHE can play a critical role in ensuring that innovation is developed, taught, and implemented equitably, helping transform health systems and expand access to life-saving solutions. #HealthEquity #HealthInnovation

    I'm excited to be in Rwanda this week to learn more about the country’s progress in health, agriculture, and digital public infrastructure. Over the last 25 years, Rwanda has delivered one of Africa’s most remarkable health transformations. The country shows what is possible when governments not only invest in life-saving technologies but focus on getting those technologies into the hands of the people who need them most. For more than two decades, the Gates Foundation has partnered with Rwanda and other countries across Africa to support them in these efforts. I'm looking forward to the conversations ahead, and to learning more from the people and institutions helping shape Africa's future.

    Alzheimer's Disease Data Initiative

    Alzheimer's Disease Data Initiative

    3d
    Bill Gates liked this
     #AAIC26 reinforced that the biggest breakthroughs in Alzheimer's research happen when data, tools and expertise are shared across institutions and borders. Two findings stood out to us: A blood test measuring p-tau217 may help predict a person's risk of cognitive decline 5 to 10 years before symptoms appear, according to a study led by Rachel Buckley that looked at data from six major research consortia. Lucia Crivelli the LatAm-FINGERS team found that a healthy lifestyle program built on the U.S. POINTER Study improved cognitive outcomes for older adults across 11 countries in Latin America, evidence that this approach can be adapted across cultures, languages and health systems. It's a great example of how the WW-FINGERS consortium, led by Miia Kivipelto, has tested and refined lifestyle interventions across diverse populations worldwide.   These kinds of findings prove what progress is possible when researchers around the world collaborate at scale. Read more: https://lnkd.in/e4zJFbPr

    I am the president of Iceland since August 1st 2024. Previously I served as the CEO and Chief Change Catalyst for The B Team, where global business and civil society leaders work together on confronting our crisis of conformity in leadership. I have long been on a quest to inspire and empower leaders to embrace purpose-driven, gender-balanced and principled leadership. I have passionately pursued this purpose as a business leader in Corporate America with M&M and Pepsi Cola, as the first female CEO of Iceland’s Chamber of commerce and as an executive and non-executive director for diverse businesses. An entrepreneur at heart, I joined the founding team of Reykjavik University where I founded the Executive Education department and led a successful initiative focused on empowering women and girls as entrepreneurs, leaders and investors. In 2007 I co-founded an investment firm with the vision to incorporate feminine values and ESG metrics into finance. The company made international headlines when it successfully survived Iceland’s infamous economic meltdown. In 2016, I ran for President as an independent candidate with no prior political experience and surprised everyone as I emerged from an initial 1% in the polls to becoming the runner-up with nearly 30% of the vote. <br><br>I have an international MBA from Thunderbird and have lived and worked in the US, the UK and across the Nordics. My work has led me to the TED stage several times and I have delivered keynotes and participated in dialogues about new visions for leadership for companies and conferences around the world. Newsweek named me to a list of 150 women who “shake the world” and the New Yorker called me a “Living Emoji of Sincerity”.
